text:
Aleksandr Petrov and Craig Macdonald’s *Effective and Efficient Training for Sequential Recommendation using Recency Sampling* (RecSys 2022) is the closest prior work. RSS samples c=max(1,⌊τn⌋) target positions with replacement, deduplicates them, and removes those interactions from the input while preserving the remaining order. Position probabilities satisfy p(k)∝α^(n−k), 0<α≤1; defaults τ=0.2, α=0.8. Multiple removed items become positives for one sequence representation. Crucially, RSS does not truncate the input before each target: later, unselected interactions can remain. Experiments apply RSS to GRU4Rec, Caser and SASRec; BERT4Rec serves as a baseline. [Paper, §§4–5](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643)

Terminal masking itself is already explicit in the original BERT4Rec paper: training includes examples masking only the last item, and inference appends a mask. That paper also discusses generating prefix/next-item examples separately for every position, describing the computational expense. Thus neither terminal masking nor prefix augmentation alone establishes novelty. [BERT4Rec, §3.6](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690)

Assessment: a policy sampling a target position, discarding its entire suffix, and predicting an appended mask from the preceding prefix differs operationally from RSS’s multiple-positive removal objective. However, recency-weighted target selection is already established by RSS, while prefix prediction and terminal masking are established by BERT4Rec. Without the proposed policy’s exact distribution, stronger novelty cannot be verified. A defensible contribution would demonstrate a distinct sampling mechanism or objective against uniform-prefix, recency-weighted-prefix, terminal-only and standard Cloze controls under matched compute; controlled experimental design alone supports an empirical contribution, not a new sampling principle.
